summary:
The “Think Differently About Emergencies Act” (Public Law 118-123) mandates that the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the Comptroller General of the United States each conduct reviews and submit reports to Congress concerning FEMA’s assistance to individuals with disabilities impacted by major disasters declared under section 401 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. 5170).

Section 2 imposes a one-time reporting requirement on the FEMA Administrator. Not later than 120 days after enactment, the Administrator must submit a report to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. The report must describe the assistance and resources FEMA provides—to States, localities, nonprofit organizations, and directly to individuals—for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their families. The required contents are: (1) a description of resources and best practices made available to those entities; (2) a detailing of the process for training and deploying personnel to coordinate with States, localities, and nonprofit organizations to meet the needs of such individuals and families; (3) a list of FEMA programs that support such individuals in preparing for and recovering from disasters, including by providing accommodations; (4) a description of FEMA’s outreach to State, local, and nonprofit experts on addressing the needs of such individuals and families; and (5) an identification of areas for improvement in supporting such individuals and families.

Section 3 requires two separate reviews, each due not later than one year after enactment. The Comptroller General and the FEMA Administrator must each: (1) review the assistance and resources FEMA provides to States, localities, nonprofit organizations, and individuals to assist individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities, individuals with physical disabilities, and their families; (2) identify potential legal impediments to providing such assistance and resources; (3) provide Congress recommendations on improving assistance and resources, enhancing coordination with States, localities, and nonprofit organizations, and streamlining the application and delivery process; and (4) provide Congress recommendations on any legislative reform necessary to improve such assistance and resources.

The Act authorizes no appropriations and creates no new programs or regulatory authorities. It establishes only discrete, time-limited reporting and review obligations.
